In addition, multimodal fusion BCI systems integrate EEG/ECoG with multimodal data such as fNIRS and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), which can achieve more accurate and efficient assistive functions. For example, a single-trial visuo-mental (VM) paradigm fNIRS-BCI system can stably decode user intent without relying on visual input, providing a more reliable and flexible non-invasive communication method for patients with advanced ALS, and has important clinical application potential. The system screens the optimal channel and hemodynamic features through statistical parameter mapping (SPM) and correlation analysis, and achieves efficient classification by combining LDA. The average accuracy rate within 4 s reaches 81.3% ± 5.7%, which is better than the traditional P3Speller’s 74.0% ± 8.9%. Further longitudinal testing on a patient in late LIS showed that the accuracy rate of fNIRS-VM still reached 73.2% ± 2.0%, which is numerically higher than the P3Speller’s 61.8% ± 1.5%.128

BCI is not currently the primary tool for early diagnosis of ALS, and the offline neurophysiological indices discussed later in discussion are assessment tools rather than true BCIs, because they are analyzed offline and are not coupled to a device or to therapeutic feedback. They nevertheless define the measurement substrate on which any future online ALS BCI would be built. Early diagnosis of ALS mainly relies on clinical manifestations and auxiliary examinations such as EMG, which often results in diagnostic delays. Offline EEG analysis combined with machine-learning classifiers has been explored for this purpose, but such pipelines are assessment tools rather than BCIs: they are analyzed offline and do not drive a device or deliver feedback. Compared with healthy individuals, patients with ALS exhibit reduced ERD amplitude and time delay in MI tasks, especially in right-sided MI. This indicates that ERD features are significantly correlated with the patient’s disease course, bulbar function, and cognitive level, providing potential biomarkers for EEG-based ALS cortical function assessment. The main goal of monitoring in ALS is to provide objective and quantifiable indices of cognitive and conscious state in patients who are completely locked in and unable to express any behavior; these indices are BCI-enabling assessment tools, not themselves BCIs. Currently, commonly used assessment methods mainly include monitoring based on motor intention decoding, monitoring based on cognitive status, and monitoring based on visual system function.106,107,110 Beyond the non-invasive indices used for monitoring and assessment, the speech neuroprostheses described above have shown that semi-invasive interfaces can support autonomous, real-time control of assistive devices in ALS; whether the same recordings can be used for reliable monitoring of neurological state and disease progression is still being investigated.131 Taken together, these EEG/fNIRS-based indices offer the prospect of an objective means of assessing cognition and consciousness in completely locked-in patients who cannot express any behavior, addressing the question of how to determine whether a completely immobile patient remains conscious. Reducing misdiagnosis as a vegetative state and informing treatment and nursing decisions remain prospective benefits; validation in large locked-in cohorts is still lacking.

BCI translation in ALS likewise has to be assessed technology by technology. Non-invasive communication BCIs (P300-, SSVEP-, and MI-based spellers) are the most clinically mature and have demonstrated feasibility for sustained, long-term home use, although this conclusion rests largely on small case series and single-subject reports rather than on large controlled trials. Invasive high-performance interfaces—ECoG- and intracortical speech or text decoders—remain predominantly investigational, with early clinical feasibility studies in small numbers of participants addressing mainly safety, device functionality, signal stability, and proof of principle. Non-invasive (EEG/fNIRS) consciousness monitoring in the complete locked-in state and ERD-based cortical assessment remain at the preclinical to early clinical stage.

sec.title: Multidimensional association between BCI and neurodegenerative diseases
sec.p: The core driving force behind the evolution of BCI comes from clinical needs: shifting from generalized symptom management toward individualized treatment based on patient-specific neural characteristics. Whether such personalization can ultimately support disease modification is not yet established, and remains an objective rather than a demonstrated outcome. Figure 7 illustrates a conceptual framework for how BCI-based neuroprotection might be organized; it depicts a proposed architecture, not a validated clinical pathway.

caption.p: The conceptual framework of BCI-driven neuroprotection

The figure contrasts the traditional, late-stage palliative care paradigm with a novel, closed-loop intervention strategy. The new paradigm leverages high-density flexible electrodes for early detection of electrophysiological anomalies, enabling multimodal data fusion and intelligent strategy optimization. This framework is proposed to enable precise, personalized interventions (e.g., multimodal sensory feedback) that may reduce neuronal damage, strengthen synaptic connections, and mitigate abnormal protein deposition, thereby potentially shifting the treatment model from reactive to proactive. As the figure indicates, these neuroprotective effects remain hypothesized and require clinical validation.

sec.p: The fundamental purpose of closed-loop monitoring is to achieve dynamic and personalized treatment. Traditional neuromodulation techniques, such as DBS and spinal cord stimulation (SCS), mainly adopt an open-loop model. Their essence is unidirectional, fixed-parameter stimulation, which cannot be dynamically adjusted according to the patient’s real-time neurophysiological state. Therefore, they have limitations such as poor adaptability, easy tolerance, and side effects.132 In contrast, the core of closed-loop BCIs lies in constructing a complete feedback loop of “real-time monitoring-decoding-intervention”: relying on implantable electrodes, optical probes, and fNIRS, a three-dimensional signal acquisition and monitoring network covering neuroelectrophysiology, inflammatory response, and metabolic state is constructed. Efficient decoding algorithms are used to identify abnormal neural activity patterns in real time and trigger precise electrical or chemical stimulation intervention within milliseconds, thus forming a bidirectional adaptive interaction mechanism. This dynamic and individualized strategy is intended to support neuroprotection: for example, adjusting stimulation parameters in real time according to the fluctuations in motor symptoms of patients with PD; such adjustment has been reported to improve symptom control while extending device battery life. Comparable closed-loop neuroprotection in other indications, such as pre-empting epileptic seizures, remains at the proof-of-concept stage and lies outside the neurodegenerative diseases reviewed here.

Recent progress in closed-loop monitoring technology has primarily focused on achieving high-precision, multi-dimensional neural signal acquisition and decoding algorithms, gradually improving real-time neural activity monitoring and prediction capabilities. Implantable electrodes, optical probes, and fNIRS can simultaneously capture a three-dimensional monitoring network of neural electrophysiological activity, local metabolic state, and the microscopic cellular environment: implantable electrodes provide high temporal resolution recording of neural electrical signals at the millisecond level, fNIRS presents a panoramic view of brain hemodynamics and metabolism at centimeter-level spatial resolution, and optical probes (such as gene-encoded calcium indicators) analyze the molecular activity of specific neuronal types at the single-cell level. Regarding implantable electrodes, although rigid electrodes (such as the classic Utah and Michigan electrodes) have demonstrated excellent conductivity, high electrode density, and signal stability in short-term applications and have been used in specific clinical scenarios such as DBS, their long-term biocompatibility and signal fidelity still have significant limitations. Flexible electrodes, due to their high biocompatibility, minimal damage, and stable signal quality, have become the focus of technological competition. For example, flexible high-density microelectrode arrays (flexible HDMEAs) are high-channel, high-spatial-resolution microelectrode arrays with electrode spacing typically less than 200 μm. Their substrates are flexible (e.g., polyimide), and this allows both high-resolution neural signal recording and electrical stimulation at the same time.133 They represent key components of a closed-loop system aimed at the real-time “reading” and “writing” of brain signals, with superior biocompatibility and long-term stability over rigid arrays.44,134 However, this material is still faced with the following problems: its flexible nature results in inadequate mechanical stiffness, which makes it difficult to implant and may damage tissue135,136,137; high-density electrodes with small footprint lead to high impedance and cross-talk of signals, hence impairing recording and stimulation performance138,139,140,141,142; stable, reliable electrical interconnection between hundreds or thousands of channels is a limiting technical challenge143,144,145; regarding long-term biocompatibility, inevitable immune responses in the body may form scar tissue which would isolate electrodes from neurons leading to poor signal over time.146 Overall, the advantages of flexible electrodes are substantial and address the fundamental limitations of rigid electrodes, whereas the advantages of rigid electrodes (such as ease of implantation and high conductivity) often reflect technological maturity and intrinsic material properties. Therefore, the evolution from rigid to flexible is an inevitable trend in BCI electrode technology toward higher biocompatibility, less trauma, and long-term stability. Novel composite materials and structural designs combining rigidity and flexibility are becoming important directions for overcoming existing bottlenecks. For example, developing “rigid-flexible composite” electrodes that maintain rigidity during implantation for ease of manipulation and regain flexibility after entering the body to adapt to tissues, or exploring new materials with both excellent electrical and mechanical properties. In terms of optical probes, current research mainly focuses on improving imaging performance and enhancing functional intelligence. NIR-II probes with deeper tissue penetration can be developed to achieve higher imaging performance by exploiting the unique optical advantages of the NIR-II window to overcome the key limitations of traditional visible light and near-infrared I probes in vivo applications, such as shallow penetration depth, strong background interference, and insufficient resolution. NIR-II fluorescent probes, with their significantly reduced tissue scattering and absorption characteristics, combined with high signal-to-noise ratio and low autofluorescence, have successfully achieved high-sensitivity in vitro detection and high-resolution in vivo imaging of deep tissues for a variety of biomarkers, covering a range of targets from tumor markers and pathogens to small molecule metabolites.147 Despite these technical advantages, the translational safety profile of NIR-II probes in humans remains poorly characterized, representing a critical barrier to clinical adoption. Biocompatibility gaps are further exacerbated by the lack of standardized human safety assessment protocols for intracranial or transdermal NIR-II probe use in neurodegenerative disease populations, who often have impaired blood-brain barrier integrity and altered systemic metabolism. NIR-II fluorescence imaging has progressed beyond the preclinical stage and has been investigated in human neurosurgical applications, including intraoperative imaging of brain gliomas.148 These first-in-human clinical studies demonstrate the feasibility of using NIR-II probes for human brain imaging and provide an important translational milestone for this technology. However, its clinical application in neurodegenerative diseases remains at an early stage, and further studies are required to establish safety, imaging performance, target specificity, and clinical utility in these populations. In terms of fNIRS, it can provide a core feedback dimension for a BCI system to achieve true closed-loop monitoring and adaptive regulation. For example, in rehabilitation training of MI BCI control function electrical stimulation (FES), studies have found that MI-BCI-FES training combined with BCI closed-loop can induce more significant brain activation (stronger ERD and HbO2 response) compared to open-loop training. The hemodynamic changes monitored in real time by fNIRS can serve as an objective indicator for quantifying the level of neural activation in training, enabling the system to dynamically adjust training parameters according to the user’s current brain state, thereby achieving personalized and adaptive neurorehabilitation. Moreover, some research has been able to detect light signals completely through the cranium in adult subjects by utilizing high power pulsed lasers and an ultra-high sensitivity detector. This approach overcomes the depth limitation of conventional fNIRS (roughly 4 cm from the brain surface), and it also provides theoretical support for the future development of new optical brain-imaging diagnostic instruments for deep brain areas such as memory, emotion, or sensation. In the decoding algorithm, the most important work is the design of an adaptive machine learning model. Adaptive machine learning algorithms on the other hand adapt continuously to changing data distribution by combining online and incremental learning modules. The fundamental idea is dynamic model adjustment with incremental learning and transfer learning, which allows a process where parameters and structure of the model are fine-tuned gradually according to newly arriving data streams, without fully retraining the model. This approach is superior to classical static models in terms of accuracy, applicability, and computational cost since it processes data instances or batch updates instantly and increases the robustness as well as reliability of the system for cases where the distribution of data changes rapidly (e.g., real-time prediction, anomaly detection). The decoding algorithm, in this manner, may also be capable of dynamically following and accommodating changes to the neural activity patterns due to the progression of a disease or daily state variability without overly relying on frequent recalibration.149 Notably, direct cross-disease transfer of decoding models across AD, PD, and ALS lacks biological plausibility given their distinct pathological substrates. Therefore, such transfer learning should be strictly limited to intra-individual calibration within the same disease entity. Only disease-non-specific technical components (e.g., adaptive calibration logic, incremental updating frameworks) can be reused across indications, whereas disease-specific biomarkers require disease-matched retraining to avoid decoding bias. Overall, the current progress in neural signal decoding algorithms is mainly reflected in the shift from “precision” to “universality” and “stability”. The next generation of BCI algorithms not only pursues high precision in an ideal laboratory environment but also strives to overcome the signal variation problem in the real world.

The mechanism most often invoked for BCI-mediated neuroplasticity is the recruitment of latent networks through neurofeedback and closed-loop feedback training. This mechanism is plausible and supported indirectly by neuroplasticity literature, but it has not been demonstrated in neurodegenerative patients; increases in synaptic strength and functional connectivity remain inferred rather than measured outcomes of BCI training.

Neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections, plays a crucial role in the recovery from neurological injury or disease. This dynamic process enables the brain to adapt to change, recover lost functions, and improve cognitive and motor skills.150 The core objective of multimodal intervention strategies is to enhance this ability, thereby altering disease progression. Traditional treatments for neurodegenerative diseases often focus on delaying neuronal death, neglecting the brain’s inherent plasticity potential. Although in the late stages of the disease, surviving neurons can partially compensate for damage through synaptic remodeling and functional reorganization, their spontaneous compensation efficiency is low and lacks targeted guidance.151,152 Multimodal intervention systems, through the intelligent matching of three intervention modes—electro, chemical, and optical—complete closed-loop feedback from pathological identification to treatment implementation. For example, modulating neural oscillations (such as 40Hz gamma oscillations) has significantly improved cognitive function for up to 8 weeks in a study of 37 patients with possible AD, compared with sham stimulation. The mechanism is to modulate gamma band oscillations and promote multi-level connectivity of brain networks: rsEEG power spectral density analysis showed that rTMS enhanced the gamma oscillation power in the left posterior temporoparietal lobe, and neuroimaging analysis further showed that 40-Hz rTMS not only prevented gray matter volume loss, but also enhanced both the local functional integration of the bilateral angular gyri and their global functional integration with the left middle frontal lobe, while strengthening the information flow from the left posterior temporoparietal lobe to the prefrontal lobe and the dynamic connectivity between the anterior and posterior brain regions.153 Multimodal BCI is intended to shift treatment from passive symptom management toward active neural function remodeling, although remodeling of this kind has so far been demonstrated only in small, short-duration studies of specific cognitive or motor protocols rather than at the disease level. It is no longer just a replacement for damaged functions, but rather a means to stimulate the brain’s own repair capabilities through precise, dynamic, and personalized closed-loop interactions, which may change the course of the disease.

The attraction of BCI technology in neurodegenerative disease lies in the possibility that an integrated closed-loop system combining monitoring, analysis, and intervention might eventually transform treatment paradigms. At present, only individual components of such a system have been realized: continuous multimodal monitoring, closed-loop stimulation for a single indication (adaptive DBS in PD), and offline decoding of disease-related signals. The fully integrated “monitoring-analysis-intervention” system described in this paragraph is a conceptual rproposal. The proposed paradigm would move beyond passive symptom relief in the later stages of disease, focusing instead on early warning, dynamic intervention, and proactive neural function remodeling, with comprehensive disease modification treated as a long-term goal rather than a demonstrated outcome. At its core is the closed-loop intelligent system. At the dynamic monitoring level, it transcends traditional sporadic imaging examinations, constructing a continuously operating multidimensional monitoring network using fNIRS technologies such as implantable electrodes and optical probes. This network can simultaneously capture neurophysiological activity, local metabolic states, and even microscopic cellular environmental changes, providing a possible data foundation for early detection of pathological changes. At the intelligent analysis and decision-making level, artificial intelligence algorithms integrate multimodal monitoring data to decode the patient’s neural activity or identify abnormal patterns in real time; in the proposed architecture, this would require capabilities well beyond those currently validated. For example, the system can analyze the synchronicity of resting-state EEG signals to warn of cognitive decline, or determine the activity of neuroinflammation through the levels of specific inflammatory factors, providing a basis for subsequent precise intervention decisions. At the level of multimodal precision intervention, the system can automatically trigger the most appropriate intervention strategy based on the analysis results. This is no longer a single electrical stimulation, but a synergistic effect of multiple means, such as electrical stimulation targeting abnormal neural oscillations, using focused ultrasound to open the blood-brain barrier for targeted drug delivery, or neuromodulation through light modulation of specific wavelengths. Integrating closed-loop monitoring, multimodal intervention, and intelligent decision-making is therefore an active research direction, with the goal of moving from static, passive symptom management toward personalized intervention. Progress toward disease modification, however, has not been demonstrated: no BCI-based intervention has yet been shown to alter the natural course of AD, PD, or ALS in a controlled trial. Should such integration eventually be achieved, it might shift the therapeutic window; whether it could alter the natural course of disease through continuous digital therapy remains speculative.

sec.title: Limitations and challenges
sec.p: BCI technology has progressed from proof-of-concept toward selected practical applications, most visibly in neurorehabilitation and assistive communication, although the number of indications supported by controlled clinical evidence remains small. However, its applications remain limited, and the market outside of medical research has not yet been fully developed. Ultimately, this can be attributed to three obstacles: technological bottlenecks, practical applications, and ethical and safety concerns, as shown in Figure 8. Table 3 summarizes in detail the major challenges and ethical issues of BCI.

caption.p: A comprehensive overview of the multifaceted challenges facing BCI technology

The diagram categorizes the major hurdles into three interconnected domains: 1) Technical Challenges, including signal processing artifacts, algorithmic limitations, individual variability, and hardware constraints; 2) Clinical and Practical Application Obstacles, encompassing performance trade-offs (e.g., speed vs. accuracy), hardware integration issues, and user experience barriers such as biocompatibility and long training periods; 3) Ethical and Privacy Challenges, focusing on informed consent, data security, responsibility attribution, and fundamental questions concerning human identity.
Major challenges and ethical issues of brain-computer interfaces (BCI)

tr.td: Technical bottlenecks
signal acquisition

signal attenuation and interference: The signal from non-invasive BCI (such as EEG) is severely attenuated when passing through the scalp and skull, and is easily interfered with by electromyography and environmental noise, resulting in a low signal-to-noise ratio.

The accuracy and stability of decoding are affected, and the continuity and effectiveness of rehabilitation training may be affected by false triggers or failure to recognize instructions. In particular, for patients with neurodegenerative diseases accompanied by motor symptoms or cognitive impairment, these limitations will directly weaken the reliability of BCI-assisted communication and neurological function recovery.

innovation in acquisition technology is needed, exploring semi-invasive or novel photon-detection interfaces to achieve a better balance between safety and signal quality; alternatively, signal-processing algorithms could be improved.
Cho et al.,154; Jafarifarmand et al.,155; Liyanage et al.156

limited information bandwidth: Current BCI technology, even the most advanced invasive electrode arrays (such as Neuralink’s “wire” electrodes), can only record the activity of hundreds to thousands of neurons simultaneously.

This limits control precision and speed, making it unsuitable for applications requiring high information density. Furthermore, high bandwidth means massive amounts of data need to be processed in real time, placing extremely high demands on the power consumption of implanted devices and wireless data transmission technology, impacting device battery life and portability.

developing high-density electrode arrays (such as flexible electrodes or graphene chips) to increase the sampling range of neurons, or novel signal acquisition technologies such as ultrasound sensing, can acquire more neural cluster activity with less invasiveness. Combining this with intelligent algorithms and closed-loop adaptive design can improve signal utilization efficiency.
Di Flumeri et al.,157; Hinrichs et al.,158; Marini et al.159
signal processing and decoding
the universality and adaptability of decoding algorithms mainly stem from large individual differences and neural plasticity during disease progression.
Pre-trained general models show decreased decoding accuracy when faced with specific patients, and system performance fluctuates as the patient’s brain adapts.

develop adaptive decoding algorithms, such as online learning or domain adaptation methods, and explore more generalizable feature representations, as well as leverage deep learning models to learn robust features from large-scale data.
Casson et al.160

limited dimensions and rate of information decoding: Basic research on how neural activity encodes complex intentions (such as specific memories and emotions) is still weak, and decoding targets are mostly limited to simple tasks (such as SSVEP and P300), making it difficult to achieve continuous and natural interaction.

Interaction scenarios are limited to discrete commands such as simple binary choices or character spelling, which cannot support continuous and natural communication that reflects true intentions. This severely limits the practical utility of BCI in improving the quality of life of late-stage patients and participating in complex cognitive rehabilitation.

on the one hand, we conduct in-depth research on the encoding logic of neural clusters for complex information, providing a biologically reasonable framework for decoding models; on the other hand, we develop hybrid encoding models and combine them with context-aware natural language processing technology to infer continuous interactive intentions from limited signals, gradually improving the naturalness and dimensionality of communication.
Chen et al.,161; Yadav et al.162
latency issue: There is a delay in the entire process from signal acquisition, processing, decoding, to the final output command.
High latency can severely impact the real-time interactive experience. For example, when controlling a wheelchair to avoid obstacles, a latency of several hundred milliseconds can be fatal.

at the hardware level, low-latency acquisition circuits and edge computing terminals are used for real-time preprocessing to reduce data transmission time. At the algorithm level, neural signals are continuously decoded in real time instead of waiting for complete data blocks, and the closed-loop response is dynamically optimized in conjunction with adaptive control strategies.
Bennett et al.,163; Islam et al.,164; Yuan et al.165
system standardization and interaction

hardware integration and compatibility: Wireless devices have limited sampling rates/channel counts; power supply and data transmission for implantable devices are unstable; imaging technologies such as fMRI are difficult to integrate with EEG systems.
Limiting the upper limit of system performance makes multimodal data fusion difficult, hindering the construction of complex, high-fidelity BCI application systems.
develop low-power, high-bandwidth application-specific integrated circuits; research wireless power transfer; and promote multimodal data fusion algorithms and standardized interfaces.
Grozea et al.,166; Yin et al.,167; Lystad et al.168

performance trade-offs: There is a conflict between the requirement for a high information transmission rate and high classification accuracy; it is difficult to balance fast system response and low false alarm rate; long-term stability and system adaptability are at odds.

This forces developers to make difficult trade-offs in system design, making it difficult to meet all high-performance indicators at the same time, thus limiting the application of BCI in safety-critical scenarios.
develop dynamic trade-off algorithms; set scenario-based performance thresholds; and adopt adaptive system design to optimize different indicators under different operating conditions.
Chen et al.,161; Yadav et al.,162; Casson et al.160
standardization and interoperability: Lack of unified hardware interface specifications and data format standards.

This leads to incompatibility between devices from different manufacturers, making it difficult to share and compare data, which greatly hinders the large-scale promotion of technology and collaborative innovation.
promote industry alliances to develop interface and data standards (such as the ONIX format); encourage the development of open-source platforms and promote interoperability.
Burwell et al.,169; Minguillon et al.170
challenges of two-way interaction (closed-loop system): Most systems are open-loop or simple closed-loop, lacking intelligent closed-loop feedback that coordinates brain, machine, and environment.

The lack of intelligent closed-loop feedback significantly weakens the accuracy and long-term efficacy of neuromodulation, making it impossible for the system to adjust in real time according to the patient’s dynamic brain state (such as disease fluctuations or neuroplasticity adaptation).

by combining multimodal signals (such as the fusion of EEG and behavioral data) to dynamically optimize the modulation strategy, adaptive neuromodulation based on individual neural states can be ultimately achieved.
Li et al.171
Practical application obstacles
user experience

the core problem lies in the cumbersome training process, followed by the impact of virtual reality integration on user experience: in VR/AR environments, BCI signals are susceptible to environmental electromagnetic interference; the closed-loop delay from signal generation to feedback from the virtual world affects immersion and interaction efficiency.

The training cycle is long and dependent on user focus; fatigue and emotional fluctuations can significantly impact performance. Some users exhibit “BCI illiteracy” because they cannot generate effective EEG signals, requiring personalized calibration. Furthermore, virtual reality integration issues reduce the realism and smoothness of the user experience, potentially causing simulator discomfort and affecting the effectiveness of BCI training and rehabilitation therapy.

optimize anti-interference circuits and signal processing algorithms; apply predictive display and other technologies to compensate for latency; design an interaction paradigm that is more tolerant of latency.
Kasahara et al.,172; Bennett et al.,163; Slobounovet al.,173; Vourvopoulos et al.174
cost and commercialization challenges

BCI equipment incurs high costs in terms of materials, procedures, and ongoing maintenance. Furthermore, the transition of BCI technology from the laboratory to industrialization faces a serious structural risk of a disconnect between technological maturity and market expectations.

In scientific research, this can lead to resource misallocation, marginalization of basic theoretical research, and even damage to academic integrity. In industry, it can spawn a large number of “pseudo-innovative” products, erode market trust, and trigger industry crises. At the social level, it can exaggerate publicity and mislead public perception, and using immature technologies on sensitive groups (such as children) can bring unpredictable ethical and safety risks.

on the technology front, hardware costs are significantly reduced through material innovation, chip integration, and large-scale production; a comprehensive governance system based on objective assessment (TRL) is established, encompassing terminology standardization, basic research, ethical governance, and multi-party collaboration, thereby guiding BCI technology toward a rational, robust, and sustainable industrialization path.
Fu et al.175
Ethical issues
doctor-patient relationship and clinical decision-making

1. privacy protection: user privacy may be leaked or maliciously manipulated, and wireless transmission technology also faces the risk of hacker attacks.2. informed consent3. right to refuse treatment4. Patient autonomy: The right to informed consent for patients with locked-in syndrome;

brain privacy differs fundamentally from traditional privacy, and BCI devices can access this more private and sensitive data. If this information is misused or leaked, it will pose a serious threat to personal dignity and even personal safety.

this requires a concerted effort across multiple levels, including law, technology, ethics, and regulation: improving the legal and regulatory framework; developing privacy-enhancing technologies; and strengthening ethical review and industry self-regulation.
Klein et al.,176; O’Brolchain et al.,177; Bonaci et al.178
end-of-life ethics issues
Patients exercise their right to terminate their lives through a brain-computer interface.

if the BCI system is subject to misreading or interference (such as signal noise or algorithm bias), it may cause patients’ true intentions to be misinterpreted as “life-ending instructions”, resulting in irreversible tragedies. At the same time, the disease itself may affect the patient’s cognitive state, making the validity of “consent” questionable.

strengthen ethical review and establish an interdisciplinary review committee. At the technical level, establish redundant verification mechanisms to ensure the system can distinguish between temporary painful impulses and stable intentions, aligning with the long-term values established by the patient while conscious, rather than relying solely on a single BCI signal output.
Poppe et al.179
attribution of responsibility

Traditional liability determination is based on “free will”, meaning that individuals control their bodily actions and bear responsibility based on their own will. However, brain-computer interface systems involve multiple potential responsible parties and may blur the boundaries between the user’s own will and technological intervention by influencing neural circuits.

when BCI devices cause users to engage in involuntary actions (such as transferring assets or signing contracts) or result in personal injury due to defects or interference, users may face legal disputes and financial losses, while developers/doctors may also be involved in litigation due to unclear liability. Furthermore, if devices are hacked, leading to privacy breaches or manipulation of behavior, it is difficult for the infringed party to trace the source, and the responsible party (developer, operator, user) is also difficult to determine.
the current legal system is not yet able to properly resolve such issues, and some scholars suggest that the responsibility should be attributed to the manufacturer.
Tamburrini et al.,180; Clausen et al.181
potential impact on personality and human nature

The continued intervention of external technologies may blur the boundaries between the inner self and external technologies; the issue of personality identity: if BCI technology can achieve large-scale memory uploading, downloading, and even editing in the future, it may shake the foundation of personality identity.

BCI may blur the lines between humans and machines, turning users into “cyborgs”; it may alter users’ self-perception or social identity; however, as a communication tool, it may restore the social participation of severely disabled individuals, thereby maintaining their personal integrity.

the key lies in guiding BCI technology toward empowerment rather than diminishing human beings. Prioritizing the protection of neurological rights, establishing value-oriented R&D principles, and engaging in broad public dialogue are all methods that can help refine the ethical boundaries of BCI technology.
Burwell et al.,169; Demetriades et al.,182; Schicktanz et al.,183; Zehr et al.184

sec.p: At the technical level, the development of BCI is mainly limited by the reliability of signal acquisition, processing, and system performance. In terms of signal acquisition, existing stimulation paradigms have obvious limitations: ERP and SSVEP require specific visual stimuli, SSVEP has a high information transmission rate but can lead to visual fatigue, and MI has a slow response speed.161,185,186,187 Hybrid BCI (such as SSVEP/ERP and SSVEP/MI) can improve robustness, but the performance is still not ideal, and multimodal signal fusion leads to high algorithm complexity.188,189,190 In addition, EEG signals acquired by non-invasive BCI are susceptible to physiological artifacts (such as eye movement and EMG) and environmental interference (such as 50/60Hz power frequency noise), resulting in a low signal-to-noise ratio.154,155,191 Various physiological factors, such as attention, memory, load, fatigue, age, gender, and location, can affect a person’s brain dynamics.172 For example, sensitive or emotional subjects may have different performance or EEG waves when performing the same task compared to enthusiastic subjects. Resting physiological parameters (i.e., resting heart rate variability, respiratory rate, and electrocardiogram) also affect the results.192,193,194 Limitations in electrode technology also affect signal quality: firstly, it is difficult to balance signal quality and ease of use in the selection of electrode materials. Wet electrodes require conductive gel, and the preparation process is cumbersome; dry electrodes are portable but have a low signal-to-noise ratio; semi-dry electrodes attempt to balance the two.157,158,195 In addition, electrode placement errors may also cause signal distortion, so the 10–20 system standard must be strictly followed.196,197 In comparison, although invasive BCI can provide higher signal quality, the surgical risks and long-term stability issues cannot be ignored.198 Signal quality and complexity also closely affect the signal processing steps. For example, the non-stationarity and individual variability of EEG signals complicate signal processing, requiring reliance on adaptive algorithms.156 Secondly, dimensionality reduction of high-dimensional EEG data is one of the core challenges of BCI systems. Although PCA and ICA are classic feature extraction methods, their linear assumptions limit their effectiveness in complex EEG signals. In the future, nonlinear models and DL need to be combined to improve the robustness of feature extraction.199,200 Linear classifiers (such as LDA) are computationally efficient but struggle to capture complex patterns, while nonlinear classifiers (such as SVM and ANN) are highly accurate but require a large amount of training data. If machine learning is applied, insufficient cross-subject generalization ability and the data requirements of DL models limit the practicality of the algorithm, while the balance between latency and accuracy in real-time processing remains an unsolved problem.163,164,165

The practical application obstacles involve whether BCI can be extended from the laboratory to real clinical applications. The core is to develop high-performance acquisition technology in system integration solutions, such as establishing stable signal acquisition and creating a theoretically robust interaction paradigm, while ensuring user safety, enhancing patient capabilities, and providing greater daily convenience.201 Among the aforementioned technical challenges, the system requires a large amount of training data for complex data processing, which leads to a problem: user experience. Approximately 15%–30% of people may not be able to generate sufficiently robust EEG signals under any circumstances. Some researchers have proposed techniques based on adaptive machine learning methods to address this issue.163 Recent adaptive machine learning frameworks specifically integrate transfer learning and domain adaptation techniques to mitigate non-stationarity and reduce calibration burden. Transfer learning leverages pre-trained models from existing users or previous sessions of the same user, fine-tuning only a small subset of parameters with limited target-subject data, which reduces the need for lengthy subject-specific calibration and improves decoding performance for novice or low-performance users. Domain adaptation further aligns the feature distributions between source (e.g., training data from healthy controls or previous sessions) and target domains (e.g., real-time data from an AD patient with cognitive fluctuations), by minimizing distributional discrepancies such as maximum mean discrepancy or adversarial training, thus maintaining decoding robustness even as the user’s neural patterns drift over time. However, the computational overhead of these methods still poses challenges for real-time edge deployment, and their generalization across diverse neurodegenerative subtypes remains unproven at scale. Meanwhile, current brain-computer interface systems generally require long training periods (typically 3–5 sessions to complete motor imagery paradigm training) and heavily rely on users’ sustained attention and emotional stability. Fatigue and emotional fluctuations can further degrade signal quality and prolong calibration time.172,194,202 Existing research mostly attributes these phenomena to individual differences in users’ neurophysiology, but a deeper systemic cause is the lack of a standardized calibration framework across laboratories: electrode placement schemes, signal preprocessing pipelines, and feature extraction thresholds vary among different research teams. This leads to calibration results that cannot be transferred across different devices for users, and some cases of “BCI illiteracy” are essentially false negatives caused by calibration mismatch. In terms of safety, the biocompatibility of invasive BCI remains to be solved. BCI requiring surgical implantation may pose a direct risk of harm to users, such as complications such as infection of surrounding tissues, acute brain trauma, or the formation of glial scars around the implant, affecting the function of the BCI. Even non-invasive BCI devices may have unknown effects on brain plasticity. Furthermore, it is unknown whether the potential side effects of BCI are reversible after device removal.180,203,204,205 To practically deploy and apply a BCI system, limitations in current hardware and performance metrics must be considered. Hardware integration faces multiple constraints: limited sampling rates and channel counts for wireless devices, unstable power supply and data transmission for implantable devices, and the difficulty in compatibility of imaging technologies such as fMRI with EEG systems.166,167,168 Performance-wise, there are conflicts between high information transmission rate requirements and classification accuracy, trade-offs between system response speed and false alarm rate, and the conflict between long-term stability and adaptive capability.160,161,162 Signal interference and latency issues in virtual-reality integration also urgently need to be addressed.173,174 In addition, the lack of unified hardware interfaces and data format standards will hinder device compatibility and large-scale deployment.169,170

From an ethical standpoint, ensuring patients’ genuine right to informed consent (especially critically ill patients with conditions such as locked-in syndrome who cannot communicate effectively) is a significant challenge. Research teams need to share moral responsibility and conduct reasonable and prudent public communication to avoid placing unrealistic expectations on patients.206,207 Furthermore, whether completely paralyzed patients should be allowed to exercise their right to terminate their lives through BCIs may also become an ethical dilemma that needs to be addressed in the future. This could paradoxically improve their quality of life and will to live, but it also requires resolving technical and ethical security issues, such as ensuring the authenticity of patients’ wishes and preventing abuse.179 Regarding privacy, BCIs may read and leak users’ thought processes (such as psychological state and personal attitudes), potentially leading to workplace discrimination or government surveillance concerns. Wireless transmission technology also faces the risk of hacker attacks, which could result in malicious manipulation of devices or leakage of sensitive information.176,177,178 The issue of liability is equally thorny; the current legal system is unable to adequately address such issues, and some scholars suggest placing responsibility on manufacturers.180,181 The potential impact of BCI on “humanity” and “personality” has also sparked controversy. Some scholars believe that BCI may blur the line between humans and machines, turning users into “cyborgs”, hybrid entities that combine organisms with mechanical or electronic systems through technological means to enhance or extend the functions of the organism. However, opponents point out that humans have long extended their capabilities through technology (such as prosthetics). The issue of personality identity is also controversial: BCI may change users’ self-perception or social identity, but some argue that such changes are no different from other medical interventions. It is worth noting that BCI, as a communication tool, may restore the social participation of severely disabled individuals, thereby maintaining their personality integrity.182,183,184,208 While BCI, as an emerging technology, is likely to raise new ethical controversies, it is essentially similar to the ethical issues (such as responsibility, risk, and side effects) encountered in traditional medicine (such as intensive care). A clear ethical framework and guidelines are crucial for the responsible use of technology and the protection of users’ rights and dignity. Although there are some lessons to be learned, most of the current discussions remain at the theoretical exploration stage and still lack concrete solutions.169

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: BCI technology, as a disruptive innovation in the field of neural engineering, is being explored across the chain of diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation of neurodegenerative diseases, with the strongest evidence so far in assistive communication and adaptive neuromodulation. This systematic review shows that BCI technology, by constructing a two-way communication bridge between the brain and the device, not only offers a potentially valuable adjunct for the earlier detection of major neurological diseases such as AD, PD and ALS, but also points toward a paradigm shift from passive symptom management toward active neural function remodeling—a shift that is currently supported mainly by early-phase clinical evidence. Its core value lies in upgrading the traditional “observation-intervention” model to an intelligent closed-loop system of “monitoring-analysis-intervention-feedback”, providing a new path for tackling the global public health challenge of neurodegenerative diseases. However, its transformation from laboratory research to routine clinical application is still in the experimental stage and is constrained by a series of multifaceted challenges. Key technical challenges include improving the biocompatibility and long-term stability of implant materials, while improving electrode and sensor design to achieve more reliable neural signal acquisition. In addition, there is an urgent need to achieve greater system miniaturization and portability while improving the overall reliability and operational stability of the device. At the computational level, research focuses on optimizing signal processing algorithms to improve the accuracy and speed of neural decoding, ensuring real-time performance in practical applications. Developing more intuitive user interfaces is also crucial for improving patient interaction and accessibility. More importantly, large-scale clinical trials are needed to generate strong evidence of clinical efficacy to validate the technology and drive its widespread adoption. Beyond technical and clinical hurdles, the responsible development and deployment of BCI technology requires addressing significant ethical and privacy issues related to neural data and fostering deeper interdisciplinary collaboration among clinicians, engineers, neuroscientists, and ethicists. To ensure the healthy development of the technology, comprehensive ethical guidelines and regulatory frameworks must be established, clearly defining standards for data privacy protection, patient rights safeguards, and technological safety. Finally, strengthening international cooperation and standardization is essential. Developing unified technical specifications and data-sharing mechanisms will facilitate the rapid translation and global adoption of BCI technology. The synergistic advancement of these research directions will collectively constitute a complete path for BCI technology to move from the laboratory to clinical application, with the potential to incrementally improve the diagnosis and treatment of neurological diseases.

By establishing direct communication between the brain and external devices, BCI has begun to influence diagnostic and therapeutic practice in neurodegenerative disease, though the change is incremental and confined to a small number of applications. This review indicates that, in early-phase studies rather than in established clinical practice, the use of BCI in Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and ALS is beginning to move from functional replacement toward functional remodeling based on neuroplasticity. Table 4 compares the three diseases across their primary clinical objectives, neural signals, major applications, evidence maturity, technical limitations, and the advantages and disadvantages of each BCI path. The shift in question lies in the construction of closed-loop systems, in which neural activity is monitored in real time and decoded output is returned as feedback. Whether such feedback stimulates the brain’s self-repair potential to an extent that reconstructs neural function is an open question; evidence is currently limited to early-phase studies of specific protocols. The combination of multimodal signal fusion and adaptive algorithms gives BCI unique advantages in early biomarker identification and personalized neuromodulation, providing a new path to overcome the global challenge of neurodegenerative diseases.

sec.p: However, the clinical application of BCI technology in the field of neurodegenerative diseases still faces multidimensional challenges. At the technical level, the reliability and stability of signal acquisition remain the core bottleneck. Non-invasive BCI is susceptible to physiological artifacts (such as eye movements and EMG) and environmental noise, resulting in a low signal-to-noise ratio. While invasive BCI can acquire high-quality neural signals, issues such as biocompatibility with long-term implantation, signal attenuation, and surgical risks have not been fully resolved. Existing stimulation paradigms (such as P300, SSVEP, and MI) each have limitations: some rely on specific sensory channels, leading to fatigue, while others have insufficient response speed; hybrid paradigms, while improving robustness, increase system complexity. At the signal processing level, the non-stationarity and individual variability of EEG signals place higher demands on feature extraction and classification algorithms. Traditional linear methods struggle to capture the complex dynamics of neural signals, while non-linear methods, such as DL, although highly accurate, face problems such as insufficient training data, weak cross-subject generalization ability, and real-time computation latency. At the clinical translation level, insufficient hardware integration, poor wireless transmission stability, and the lack of a unified data interface standard limit the systematic deployment of BCI. Furthermore, user experience is a significant limiting factor, with approximately 15–30% of users exhibiting “BCI illiteracy”, being unable to generate effective signals. System performance is also susceptible to fatigue, fluctuations in attention, and emotional states, further restricting its widespread adoption. Ethical and security challenges are equally undeniable. The long-term security of invasive BCI remains unclear; the risks of cognitive privacy breaches, data security breaches, and hacking highlight the urgency of protecting neural data; and issues such as informed consent from severely disabled patients, altered identity, and attribution of responsibility require further discussion within a legal and ethical framework.

A possible future trajectory for BCI in neurodegenerative disease is an extension beyond functional replacement toward neuromodulation that senses, analyzes and intervenes dynamically; this trajectory is a research direction rather than an established outcome, and progress depends on the evidence reviewed above. The core of this transformation lies in achieving a leap from open-loop assistance to closed-loop regulation. Future BCI may no longer be limited to converting brain signals into external device commands, but will instead focus on real-time monitoring of pathological activities in specific neural circuits (such as excessively synchronized beta oscillations in PD or characteristic gamma wave abnormalities in AD), and implementing precise neural modulation accordingly. The realization of this adaptive system requires overcoming millisecond-level signal processing delays, developing targeted stimulation strategies based on individual brain network characteristics, and establishing an intelligent algorithm system capable of dynamically adjusting parameters as the disease progresses. Faced with the high heterogeneity of neurodegenerative diseases, BCI technology needs to deepen its development toward multimodal fusion and personalized intervention. A single signal modality is insufficient to comprehensively capture the complex pathophysiological processes of diseases; future development requires integrating multi-dimensional information such as electrophysiology, blood flow metabolism, and molecular imaging to construct a dynamic disease atlas across scales. By combining high temporal resolution EEG signals with high spatial resolution imaging data, BCI systems hold the promise of identifying specific neural network dysfunctions in the very early stages of disease and tailoring intervention plans for patients with different clinical subtypes. This means that BCI will transform from a general-purpose tool into a personalized diagnostic and treatment platform that can adapt to individual brain characteristics, disease stages, and even daily fluctuations in condition. Although this review focuses on neurodegenerative diseases, the closed-loop principles are conceptually transferable to psychiatric disorders such as treatment-resistant depression and autism, where similar biomarker-driven closed-loop paradigms are under investigation.209 However, achieving widespread clinical application of BCI still requires overcoming multiple challenges from technology validation to clinical application. These include demonstrating its disease-modifying effects in delaying disease progression through large-scale clinical trials, developing low-cost, easy-to-operate hardware systems suitable for home environments, and establishing an ethical and regulatory framework that keeps pace with technological innovation. Particular attention needs to be paid to the impact of long-term brain-computer interaction on neuroplasticity, the privacy and security boundaries of neural data, and ethical and social issues such as informed consent mechanisms for severely disabled patients. Crucially, these challenges—ranging from signal stability and biocompatibility to data governance—are not confined to neurodegeneration; they represent universal hurdles equally pertinent to psychiatric BCI applications, thereby validating the cross-disease applicability of the roadmap proposed herein. Only through the deep integration of neuroscience, clinical medicine, engineering, and ethics can BCI technology truly become a key force driving the transformation of precision diagnosis and treatment for neurodegenerative diseases.
